title: Jatayu in the Ramayana: His Fight and Shri Ram's Grace
description: Who is Jatayu? Read about his friendship with Shri Ram, his fight during Mata Sita's abduction, and the devotion he asks for in Aranya Kand.
answer: Jatayu is the king of vultures who befriends Shri Ram and fights during Ravan's abduction of Mata Sita. In the Ramcharitmanas, Goswami Tulsidas describes how Shri Ram comforts the wounded Jatayu, grants him His grace and performs his funeral rites. Jatayu asks for uninterrupted devotion before ascending to the Lord's abode.

sections.md:
The Lord receives Jatayu as a friend. In Aranya Kand, doha 13, Goswami Tulsidas describes Shri Ram meeting the king of vultures and developing friendship with him. Shri Ram then stays near the Godavari, where He makes a hut of leaves. Jatayu thus enters the account through friendship before we read of his suffering.

**Service grows from love.** Jatayu later fights during Ravan's abduction of Mata Sita, in the Aranya Kand account leading to doha 30. His friendship takes the form of action when she is in danger. We can begin here in understanding his devotion: love for Shri Ram gives him a reason to act.

sections.h2: Shri Ram comforts the wounded Jatayu
sections.md:
Jatayu's suffering receives the Lord's personal care. In Aranya Kand, doha 30, Shri Ram strokes his head with His own hands. As Jatayu gazes upon Shri Ram's face, his pain disappears. Goswami Tulsidas presents the Lord as the ocean of mercy, showing that His compassion reaches the wounded bird directly.

**Devotion does not make suffering a measure of failure.** One may question how a faithful servant can be left wounded. Jatayu's account acknowledges his pain and then shows Shri Ram tending to him. We should read both parts together. His wounds are real, and so is the Lord's care. The next part of the account reveals what Jatayu himself desires from Him.

Jatayu asks that his devotion continue without interruption. In Aranya Kand, the opening chaupai associated with doha 32 describes him leaving his vulture body and receiving a divine form resembling Shri Hari, with four arms and yellow garments. With tears in his eyes, he praises the Lord.

**His chosen boon is devotion.** Aranya Kand, doha 32, then records his request and his ascent to Shri Hari's abode. Shri Ram performs his funeral rites with His own hands. The Lord's friendship extends through this final act of care. As we read, we can dwell on Jatayu's request and make continuity in devotion part of our own daily practice.

faq.a: Yes. Aranya Kand, doha 13, identifies Jatayu as the king of vultures and describes his friendship with Shri Ram. His bodily form places no barrier before the Lord's affection. In Aranya Kand, doha 32, Shri Ram personally performs his funeral rites after Jatayu ascends to Shri Hari's abode.

faq.q: What did Shri Ram do for Jatayu?
faq.a: In Aranya Kand, doha 30, Shri Ram strokes Jatayu's head with His hands, and Jatayu's pain disappears as he looks upon Him. Aranya Kand, doha 32, records Jatayu's ascent to Shri Hari's abode after asking for uninterrupted devotion. Shri Ram then performs his funeral rites with His own hands.

Yes. Uttar Kand, in the chaupai associated with doha 67b, identifies Sampati as Jatayu's elder brother. Kakbhushundi recounts how the search party sent south in search of Mata Sita meets Sampati. After hearing his news, Hanumanji leaps across the ocean and makes his way into Lanka.
